ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were randomly assigned to view two short TikTok-style inoculation videos addressing common myths about an HIV vaccine, or attention-matched control videos on nutrition and diabetes.

> Intervention participants were also more likely to recommend the vaccine (+0.74; 95% CI 0.61, 0.88; p<0.01).

> We recruited participants from Prolific, an online research platform that includes thousands of individuals from South Africa. 22 We enrolled participants who were female, aged 18-29 years, resident in South Africa, and able to read English (as indicated by Prolific as 'fluent in English'); and had had sex in the past 12 months and reported their HIV status as negative or unknown.

> Although Prolific participants tend to be more educated than the general population in South Africa, the platform enabled rapid recruitment of a large, relevant cohort of young women who would be eligible for an HIV vaccine.

> Prolific invited eligible users to participate and provided a link to the study survey, which was administered through Qualtrics.

> To reduce the potential for demand-side characteristics to explain the results, all participants were provided with information about the HIV vaccine prior to randomisation to the intervention or control group: that any HIV vaccine available to the public in the future would have been tested and found to be safe and effective.

> Participants were then randomly assigned (1:1) to the intervention and control groups.

> After viewing the videos, all participants were shown the two primary misinformation claims -those directly addressed in the inoculation videos -presented as Facebook posts (see appendix 3 (p 20).

> Participants were shown the two primary misinformation claims again, along with four new misinformation claims and one new true claim, and completed the same set of outcome measures, including HIV vaccine intentions and HIV vaccine recommendation.

> Specifically, participants were asked: "If an HIV vaccine became available, how likely would you be to get vaccinated?"

> Between 24 July and 16 October 2025 we enrolled 2,163 participants, representing 93% of eligible individuals invited to participate (See CONSORT diagram, Figure 2).

> Overall, the mean age was 25 years (standard deviation (SD): 2.57) and participants were predominantly Black African (91%).

> Controlling for covariates (Figure 3 Panel A and appendix 1 (p 2, Table S2), intervention group participants were more likely to recommend the HIV vaccine to a friend than control group participants (+0.74, p<0.01, 95%CI: 0.61,0.88).

> We do however know that the study intervention reduced how much people believed misinformation, and misinformation has been found to be associated with reduced vaccine uptake. 5, 28 Second, participants were recruited through an online research platform and may not fully reflect the broader population of adolescent girls and young women in South Africa.

> Although nearly all participants were daily social media users the generalisability of our findings to offline or harder-to-reach populations requires further study.

> We are confident that the effects found in the main survey are caused by the intervention given that only 29 participants were asked to rewatch the video, and that the main survey results are robust to the exclusion of these participants.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: Participants were randomly assigned to view two short TikTok-style inoculation videos addressing common myths about an HIV vaccine, or attention-matched control videos on nutrition and diabetes.
Intervention participants were also more likely to recommend the vaccine (+0.74; 95% CI 0.61, 0.88; p<0.01).

We recruited participants from Prolific, an online research platform that includes thousands of individuals from South Africa. 22 We enrolled participants who were female, aged 18-29 years, resident in South Africa, and able to read English (as indicated by Prolific as 'fluent in English'); and had had sex in the past 12 months and reported their HIV status as negative or unknown.

Although Prolific participants tend to be more educated than the general population in South Africa, the platform enabled rapid recruitment of a large, relevant cohort of young women who would be eligible for an HIV vaccine.
Prolific invited eligible users to participate and provided a link to the study survey, which was administered through Qualtrics.

To reduce the potential for demand-side characteristics to explain the results, all participants were provided with information about the HIV vaccine prior to randomisation to the intervention or control group: that any HIV vaccine available to the public in the future would have been tested and found to be safe and effective.
Participants were then randomly assigned (1:1) to the intervention and control groups.
After viewing the videos, all participants were shown the two primary misinformation claims -those directly addressed in the inoculation videos -presented as Facebook posts (see appendix 3 (p 20).

Participants were shown the two primary misinformation claims again, along with four new misinformation claims and one new true claim, and completed the same set of outcome measures, including HIV vaccine intentions and HIV vaccine recommendation.
Specifically, participants were asked: "If an HIV vaccine became available, how likely would you be to get vaccinated?"
Between 24 July and 16 October 2025 we enrolled 2,163 participants, representing 93% of eligible individuals invited to participate (See CONSORT diagram, Figure 2).
Overall, the mean age was 25 years (standard deviation (SD): 2.57) and participants were predominantly Black African (91%).

Controlling for covariates (Figure 3 Panel A and appendix 1 (p 2, Table S2), intervention group participants were more likely to recommend the HIV vaccine to a friend than control group participants (+0.74, p<0.01, 95%CI: 0.61,0.88).

We do however know that the study intervention reduced how much people believed misinformation, and misinformation has been found to be associated with reduced vaccine uptake. 5, 28 Second, participants were recruited through an online research platform and may not fully reflect the broader population of adolescent girls and young women in South Africa.
Although nearly all participants were daily social media users the generalisability of our findings to offline or harder-to-reach populations requires further study.

We are confident that the effects found in the main survey are caused by the intervention given that only 29 participants were asked to rewatch the video, and that the main survey results are robust to the exclusion of these participants.

text.text: Misinformation decreases public confidence in health technologies and willingness to use them.
Psychological inoculation, or "prebunking", exposes people to misleading claims before they spread widely and refutes the claims and embedded persuasion tactics.
Evidence on its effectiveness for HIV-related misinformation, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa and among young women (a population highly vulnerable to HIV), is limited.
We conducted a randomised controlled trial (July to October 2025) among 2,163 women aged 18-29 years recruited online in South Africa.
Participants were randomly assigned to view two short TikTok-style inoculation videos addressing common myths about an HIV vaccine, or attention-matched control videos on nutrition and diabetes.
All participants then viewed multiple false claims presented as social media posts.
The primary outcome was intention to receive an HIV vaccine if available (1-10 scale), assessed immediately postintervention and at three-week follow-up.
Secondary outcomes included likelihood of recommending the vaccine; and perceived credibility, emotional impact, and shareability of misinformation claims.
We used linear regression models to estimate intervention effects.
Misinformation exposure reduced vaccine intentions by 0.63 points in the control group, while intentions increased by 0.30 points in the intervention group.
Controlling for covariates and baseline intentions, post-exposure vaccine intentions were 0.92 points higher in the intervention group (95% CI 0.78, 1.06; p<0.01), a 12% relative increase.

text.text: Brief, scalable psychological inoculation delivered via social-media-style videos protected young women's HIV vaccine intentions, with effects generalising to novel claims and persisting over three weeks.
Prebunking campaigns may safeguard public confidence in other new HIV prevention technologies like lenacapavir.

Expanded HIV prevention and treatment services across sub-Saharan Africa over the past 20 years has enabled millions to live longer, healthier lives, yet HIV incidence remains highparticularly among adolescent girls and young women.

Many prevention efforts have had only modest success, with low uptake and low sustained use of effective prevention options like oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) among young women. 1 As a result, the development of new prevention options, including an HIV vaccine, remains important for ending the HIV epidemic.

text.text: The recent discovery of highly-effective long-acting injectable PrEP represents a major opportunity to accelerate progress toward an HIV-free generation.

Among new modalities, lenacapavir is the first twice-yearly injectable PrEP shown to offer substantial protection against HIV acquisition. 2 Lenacapavir has received swift global support, including World Health Organization prequalification and record-speed approval in South Africa. 3, 4 While ensuring adequate supply of new biomedical innovations like lenacapavir is a prerequisite for altering the trajectory of the HIV epidemic, addressing the barriers to demand for such innovations is equally important.

text.text: Prior experience with innovations like COVID-19 and human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccines has demonstrated how viral misinformationespecially regarding safety, ingredients, and scientific and policymaker intent -can erode public confidence and significantly undermine uptake. [5] [6] [7] Identifying effective and scalable approaches to countering misinformation about new health products -particularly before it becomes viral and widespread -is thus an important priority for policymakers and public health practitioners.

text.text: We investigated psychological inoculation as a strategy to proactively build resistance to HIV prevention misinformation, focusing here on a yet-to-be developed HIV vaccine.

Analogous to medical inoculation, psychological inoculation entails exposing individuals to weakened versions of misinformation or misleading arguments, alongside refutations or explanations that highlight the common fallacies and manipulative tactics used in misinformation campaigns. 8, 9 This "prebunking" process aims to build cognitive resistance among individuals before they encounter stronger, more persuasive forms of misinformation -it gets ahead of misinformation before it can do damage. 8 Figure 1 depicts the theory of psychological inoculation.

text.text: Prebunking may be more effective than debunking, which counters false claims after they've already spread and taken hold, because of the continued influence effect: the psychological phenomenon where outdated or false information continues to influence a person's thinking and decision-making even after it has been corrected or retracted. 11 Prior research in other domains has shown that brief (5-15 minute) interactive prebunking interventions, often delivered via online games, can reduce belief in misinformation and reduce willingness to share them. 12 Meta-analyses also support the efficacy of psychological inoculation. 12, 13 However, psychological inoculation has been studied primarily in highincome countries and for topics including COVID-19, 14, 15 climate change, 16 and politics. 17 There is limited evidence on the use of psychological inoculation for HIV-related misinformation, from low-and middle-income countries, and among young people. 18, 19 Furthermore, little is known about the effectiveness of brief, social-media-native video formats (e.g., TikTok's distinct portrait-orientation reels) in delivering psychological inoculation at scale, which is an important gap in light of high social media penetration globally.

text.text: To address these gaps, we developed and tested two 2.5-minute videos that sought to inoculate viewers against common misinformation claims about a future HIV vaccine.
We then conducted a pre-registered, two-arm randomised controlled trial with 2,163 women (18-29 years old) in South Africa.

Our trial tested several pre-registered hypotheses: 1) participants who viewed the inoculation videos prior to exposure to misleading claims would report higher intentions to receive the HIV vaccine and be more likely to recommend the vaccine to a friend -an indicator of broader normative acceptance; 2) the inoculation videos would reduce the perceived credibility, emotional impact, and shareability of misinformation claims; 3) psychological inoculation would generalise to different misinformation claims and tactics not explicitly addressed in the videos; 4) the intervention would remain effective after 3-4 weeks.
We conducted a two-arm randomised controlled trial consisting of a main online survey (at study enrolment) and a follow-up survey approximately three weeks later.

The main survey included: delivery of the intervention videos (or attention-matched control videos); exposure to multiple misinformation claims; pre-and post-intervention measurement of the primary outcome of vaccine intentions; and a study debrief highlighting that all misinformation claims were fabricated for research purposes.
The follow-up survey included: exposure to additional misinformation claims; a re-assessment of vaccine intentions to examine the persistence of effects over time; and another study debrief.

We recruited participants from Prolific, an online research platform that includes thousands of individuals from South Africa. 22 We enrolled participants who were female, aged 18-29 years, resident in South Africa, and able to read English (as indicated by Prolific as 'fluent in English'); and had had sex in the past 12 months and reported their HIV status as negative or unknown.

text.text: Although Prolific participants tend to be more educated than the general population in South Africa, the platform enabled rapid recruitment of a large, relevant cohort of young women who would be eligible for an HIV vaccine.
Prolific invited eligible users to participate and provided a link to the study survey, which was administered through Qualtrics.
Participants could complete the survey on any internet-enabled device.
After providing informed consent, participants answered questions related to socio-economic characteristics, mental health, and prior health behaviours.
The survey also assessed participants' HIV vaccine intentions and likelihood of recommending the HIV vaccine.

To reduce the potential for demand-side characteristics to explain the results, all participants were provided with information about the HIV vaccine prior to randomisation to the intervention or control group: that any HIV vaccine available to the public in the future would have been tested and found to be safe and effective.
Participants were then randomly assigned (1:1) to the intervention and control groups.
Randomisation and survey administration were fully automated.
Participants in the intervention group viewed two short inoculation videos, which were developed in three steps.
First, we conducted a rapid review of misinformation claims about HIV vaccines (details published elsewhere), 23 identifying concerns around side effects, fertility, and conspiracy theories.

text.text: Second, we selected 54 unique claims from the review and surveyed young South African women (18-29 years; n=188) to determine which claims were most concerning to them.

Safety-related claims -particularly those suggesting severe harm -were rated most concerning (details published elsewhere). 24 Third, we developed a new set of false HIV-vaccine safety claims incorporating commonly used persuasion tactics when promoting misinformation. 25 The claims mimic real-world statements that people could encounter.

text.text: We tested their perceived credibility and influence on vaccine intentions and recommendations in a second online survey (n=195).
The two claims selected for the intervention scored highly in this second survey for how concerning, credible, and shareable they were; making them good candidates for inoculation.
The first claim is "My sister got the HIV vaccine and her heart stopped the next day.
Please don't get vaccinated-IT COULD KILL YOU!

This claim uses the post hoc fallacy, a misinformation tactic that exploits the human tendency to infer a cause-and-effect relationship based solely on the temporal order of events. 25 The second claim is "HIV vaccine?!

This claim uses a misinformation tactic called "impossible expectations", which is based on demanding unrealistic standards before acting on scientific evidence. 25 Scripts for videos that inoculated against these two claims were developed following the three-part structure (see Figure 1): threat activation (alerting viewers that misinformation is common and about a specific false claim); refutation of the claim by explaining the common fallacies and manipulative tactics used in the claim; and a call to action (encouragement to look out for misinformation).

text.text: The scripts were developed via participatory prototyping with young women (19-25 years old) in South Africa working as peer ambassadors for a mobile health clinic.

Based on formative work assessing multiple modes or formats of inoculation content delivery (whiteboard animation, digital avatar, live video, or text), we then scripted and produced brief multi-character TikTok style videos filmed by a South African production company.

Co-design workshops with peer health navigators and counselors from an HIV service delivery organisation helped ensure that the content, format, and actor choice were locally relevant, salient, and relatable.

text.text: We also incorporated several strategies from the behavioural economics toolkit to strengthen message engagement, comprehension, retention, and to motivate action.

Each video was followed by a short comprehension quiz (see appendix 2 (pp 16-19); incorrect answers required viewing the videos again since we sought to ensure that participants understood the tactics used in misinformation claims and thereby test the efficacy of psychological inoculation. 26 Other strategies included cognitive engagement with the material through selection of a digital sticker at the end of the main survey; priming a new identity for the participants as misinformation spotters; and reminder SMS messages between the main and follow-up surveys to prompt sharing their new expertise in countering misinformation.

text.text: Participants in the control arm viewed two attention-matched videos of identical length and style, and produced with the same actor, that focused on nutrition and diabetes, but with no inoculation content.
After viewing the videos, all participants were shown the two primary misinformation claims -those directly addressed in the inoculation videos -presented as Facebook posts (see appendix 3 (p 20).

Immediately after each post, participants rated (a) its credibility, (b) the extent to which it made them anxious or worried about an HIV vaccine, and (c) their likelihood of sharing it on social media.
HIV vaccine intentions were then measured a second time to assess the impact of misinformation exposure on the primary outcome.
Next, participants viewed four additional misinformation claims and one true claim, presented in random order.
For each claim, the same three outcomes -credibility, anxiety, and shareability -were assessed.

The additional false claims were included to assess the extent to which the psychological inoculation might generalise beyond the HIV claims that were specifically inoculated against to new claims that used different content and tactics.
HIV vaccine recommendation was measured again at the end of this sequence to capture changes after exposure to the full set of claims.
The follow-up survey was administered approximately three weeks later (median: 21 days; average: 22.6; SD: 5.4).

Participants were shown the two primary misinformation claims again, along with four new misinformation claims and one new true claim, and completed the same set of outcome measures, including HIV vaccine intentions and HIV vaccine recommendation.
The study ended with a second debrief identical to the main survey debrief.
The primary outcome was participants' intention to get vaccinated.
Specifically, participants were asked: "If an HIV vaccine became available, how likely would you be to get vaccinated?"
(1-10 scale, where 1 is extremely unlikely and 10 is extremely likely).
Given that an HIV vaccine is not yet available, our measure proxied actual demand for the vaccine.
A secondary outcome assessed participants' likelihood of recommending the vaccine to friends ("If an HIV vaccine became available, how likely would you be to recommend it to your friends?"
; 1-10 scale).

Additional secondary outcomes measured on 1-7 scales assessed the extent to which participants believed the claims ("How much do you believe this post is true?") ; the anxiety induced by these claims ("How much does this post make you anxious or worried about the HIV vaccine?") ; and the likelihood of sharing the claims ("If you saw this post on social media, how likely would you be to share it?").

We used ordinary least squares regression (OLS) models to estimate the effect of the intervention on primary and secondary outcomes, controlling for demographic, socioeconomic and other factors that have previously been shown to influence vaccine intentions and the perceived credibility of misinformation.

These were participants' age, race, education, province of residence (i.e., Gauteng or other), residential setting (i.e., informal settlement/township or other), employment status, and food insecurity.
Province is relevant as the young people who co-designed the intervention resided in Gauteng province.
While the intervention was designed for all young people in South Africa, it is possible it resonated more with people living in Gauteng.

We also controlled for participant characteristics such as daily use of social media; symptoms of depression (i.e., PHQ-2 score ≥3); no receipt of a COVID-19 vaccine (proxy for being vaccine hesitant); ever used PrEP; HIV risk perception (binary variable identifying self-perceived high HIV risk); information avoidance behaviour (above the median); and self-reported confidence in scientists (1-4 scale).
Finally, we also controlled for the pre-intervention values of the outcome variables in the regression specifications.

We also conducted pre-specified subgroup analyses to examine whether the effect of the intervention on study outcomes differed by age (<25 years vs. ≥25 years), prior PrEP use (never used vs. ever used), perceived risk of HIV (low vs. high), COVID-19 vaccination status (never received vs. received at least one dose), and information avoidance behaviour (low vs. high).

text.text: For each sub-group characteristic, a separate analysis was conducted by including an interaction term between the treatment indicator and the corresponding binary subgroup indicator in a regression model that included the full sample.
This interaction term tested whether the intervention effect differed significantly between a given subgroup and its complement.

Effectiveness within a subgroup was defined as the magnitude and direction of the intervention effect in that subgroup, and a subgroup was characterised as showing greater effectiveness than its complement when the interaction term was statistically significant and indicated a larger treatment effect in that subgroup.
All analyses were conducted using Stata version 16.1.
The funder of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation, or writing of the report.

text.text: Overall, the mean age was 25 years (standard deviation (SD): 2.57) and participants were predominantly Black African (91%).

Education levels were high with 99% having completed high school (grade 12), but other measures indicated variation in socioeconomic status: 11% reported household hunger (past 7 days), and over a third were living in a township or informal settlement.
Nearly all participants reported daily social media use and about half resided in Gauteng Province, the largest province in South Africa.
Participants' intentions to take the HIV vaccine were similar in both groups: mean of 7.81 and 7.77 in the control and intervention groups respectively.
HIV vaccine intentions decreased in the control group after seeing the misinformation claims (-0.63, SD:1.92).
In contrast, intentions to take the vaccine increased in the intervention group after seeing the inoculation video and then being shown the misinformation claims (+0.30, SD:1.82).

text.text: In this randomised controlled trial with young women in South Africa, brief psychological inoculation messages delivered through short videos were effective in protecting participants from the negative effects of misinformation about a yet-to-be-developed HIV vaccine.
The inoculation messages prevented the substantial decline in intentions to accept an HIV vaccine observed in the control group after encountering misinformation.

The intervention also reduced the perceived credibility of multiple misinformation claims, lowered negative emotional reactions to misinformation, and decreased participants' likelihood of sharing false claims.
Importantly, these protective effects persisted three weeks later, even after participants saw a broader range of misinformation claims.
Together, these findings show that inoculation messages can meaningfully preserve vaccine intentions and reduce susceptibility to misinformation in a population particularly at risk of acquiring HIV.
Furthermore, the protective effects of the inoculation videos extended beyond the two specific claims about the HIV vaccine addressed in the videos.

The additional claims included ones using the same persuasion tactics as in the main claims (post hoc fallacy and impossible expectations) but with different content and in relation to vaccines in general, the flu vaccine, and different health topics.
They also included claims using different persuasion tactics and about other vaccines or HIV prevention methods.

Inoculated participants also rated these new claims as less credible, experienced lower levels of worry in response to them, and reported a lower likelihood of sharing them compared to the control group.
This is an encouraging finding given how rapidly false claims evolve and how difficult it is to preemptively counter every claim that may emerge.
It points to the potential for concise, scalable inoculation interventions to offer broader protection against misinformation.

While we found no evidence that the inoculation videos made participants more suspicious of accurate health claims immediately after receiving the intervention, at the 3-week follow-up the intervention group was slightly less likely than the control group to believe that smoking increases risk of lung cancer but that not everyone who smokes gets lung cancer.
This result could indicate a small backfire effect of inoculation that should be considered in future studies and intervention delivery.

One explanation for this finding, however, is that the claim included language that might have been seen to be consistent with the persuasion technique of impossible expectations ("increases your risk of lung cancer for sure"), which was the focus of the second inoculation video.
The intervention group may have become more skeptical about posts that make absolute claims.
Another explanation is that the inoculation videos' call to action -to trust only credible sources -may have led participants to distrust a Facebook post by "Slay Queen."
Finally, there is potential that the intervention group found this claim suspicious given the true claim had nothing to do with the intervention or misinformation topic (the HIV vaccine).

Our main survey results are consistent with findings of a recent meta-analysis, 12 which found that psychological inoculation improved the ability to identify manipulative content specifically rather than increasing generalized scepticism.

text.text: There are several mechanisms through which brief, engaging inoculation videos may have combatted misinformation.

First, consistent with the inoculation (prebunking) approach and given the HIV vaccine is not available yet, participants most likely had not yet formed strong opinions or preferences related to the HIV vaccine nor had been exposed to many claims about it.
This highlights the importance of getting out ahead of misinformation when a new health technology is being introduced.

Second, the protection/immunity found in our study beyond the specific claims we inoculated against is consistent with the theoretical proposition that inoculation against underlying argumentative tactics, rather than against specific factual assertions, can build a broader cognitive immune response. 12 Third, the intervention videos used a familiar, highly engaging social-media format and incorporated multiple behavioural insights to increase attention, salience, and relatability.

text.text: This points to the importance of ensuring the potency and relatability of brief video interventions like ours to enable broad dissemination.

To our knowledge, this is the first psychological inoculation study to focus specifically on HIV prevention in sub-Saharan Africa -an important context given the high burden of HIV and the rapid diffusion of health misinformation through social media.

Our findings contribute to an emerging literature on the effectiveness of prebunking interventions in mitigating the influence of misinformation, while extending this literature into the domain of HIV prevention in a middle-income country setting.

Two previous studies have assessed the impact of psychological inoculation on condom use and disclosure among people living with HIV. 18, 19 While other inoculation studies demonstrating significant effects typically have more intensive and active inoculation (e.g., playing an interactive game), our light touch, passive inoculation intervention (watching two 2.5-minute videos) achieved similar results in a format that is easily scalable.

text.text: This study has several limitations.
First, we assessed participants' vaccine intentions rather than actual health behaviour.
Because an HIV vaccine does not yet exist, measuring stated demand is the most feasible proxy for potential uptake, and the hypothetical context is valid for the intervention and control groups.
The use of intention measures is common in online experimental studies, but the extent to which intentions translate into real-world behaviour remains uncertain.

We do however know that the study intervention reduced how much people believed misinformation, and misinformation has been found to be associated with reduced vaccine uptake. 5, 28 Second, participants were recruited through an online research platform and may not fully reflect the broader population of adolescent girls and young women in South Africa.

text.text: Although nearly all participants were daily social media users the generalisability of our findings to offline or harder-to-reach populations requires further study.

Our findings may nonetheless apply more broadly as psychological inoculation effects have been found to be similar across education levels. 29 In addition, we found that our intervention had similar effects on HIV-vaccine intentions among those residing in an informal settlement/township and those living elsewhere.

text.text: This finding provides some confidence that results may apply to young women across a broader socioeconomic spectrum.

We also found that 36.3% of our study participants reported a "moderate" or "great risk" of HIV infection, indicating our sample is the population of interest when rolling out HIV prevention services.
Third, we cannot isolate the effect of the inoculation videos completely from the effect of the other intervention components.
One concern with the main study findings is that this could be driven by intervention participants answering the quiz questions incorrectly and being asked to rewatch the video.

We are confident that the effects found in the main survey are caused by the intervention given that only 29 participants were asked to rewatch the video, and that the main survey results are robust to the exclusion of these participants.
The identity prime at the end of the main survey and SMS reminder before the follow-up might have boosted the intervention effect slightly at follow-up.
While future research should isolate the inoculation impact, it is likely that nudges such as these have relatively small effects in comparison to the main intervention.
Fourth, our follow-up period was limited to approximately three weeks (which is longer than many inoculation studies that do not include a follow-up).
While we observed encouraging durability over this interval, longer-term assessments are needed to determine whether the protective effects of inoculation persist as misinformation evolves.

Fifth, while the control group received the same information about the HIV vaccine as provided to the intervention group in the inoculation videos -any HIV vaccine available to the public in the future would have been tested and found to be safe and effective -it is possible that the results could, in part, be explained by demand-side characteristics.
Sixth, we do not know whether our results would generalise to other country contexts with lower prevalence of HIV.
Although an HIV vaccine is not yet available, there are ongoing efforts to develop a safe and effective vaccine.

Equipping people with the ability to detect and reject false claims before health products become widely available is essential for ensuring high demand, given mounting evidence that debunking misinformation after it has spread is much more difficult and often less effective. 30 Our findings are also extremely timely in light of the imminent rollout of lenacapavir, a groundbreaking long-acting medication for HIV prevention that is very likely to be the subject of considerable misinformation about its safety, biological mechanisms, and the populations for which it is intended.
